newsitem.title: CHINA: China, U.S. agree to further military ties.
newsitem.headline: China, U.S. agree to further military ties.

text.p: U.S. General John Shalikashvili and China's top brass on Tuesday agreed during talks in Beijing to develop military ties, frozen when Chinese soldiers crushed pro-democracy demonstrations in 1989.

Shalikashvili, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, arrived in China on Monday for a visit until May 16 at the invitation of General Fu Quanyou, chief of staff of the People's Liberation Army (PLA).

Shalikashvili, the most senior U.S. military officer to visit China since 1983, met Fu and was to hold meetings with Vice-Premier and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and generals Zhang Wannian and Chi Haotian, vice-chairmen of the Communist Party's Central Military Commission.

"During talks, the two sides expressed a positive attitude toward continuing military exchanges and furthering military ties," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing. Shalikashvili met Fu for talks on Tuesday morning.
"We are willing to see the strengthening of Sino-U.S. military ties," Shen said.
Shalikashvili was scheduled to visit military facilities and units and to speak to the PLA's National Defence University in Beijing.
U.S. officials have said the trip is aimed at strengthening ties and increasing understanding and transparency between the world's most powerful and most heavily manned militaries.

A number of Western countries have recently moved to improve military relations with the three-million strong PLA that were effectively frozen in 1989 when soldiers crushed student-led pro-democracy protests in Beijing with heavy loss of life.

Shalikashvili's visit was the latest in a series by senior U.S. officials to China. The visits have helped warm the cross-Pacific relationship, long strained by disputes over issues ranging from human rights to trade to Taiwan.
